voice: Ḍombīpāda sings a ferry song: he watches the Mātaṅgī girl at her crossing and, in the refrain, calls to Ḍombī the way a boatman urges on a rower (Munidatta hears the singer urging himself). Plain English on the beat of oar strokes: brisk in the calls, riddling in couplet 4, blunt at the end.

lines.en: the [Mātaṅgī]{matangi} girl, plunged in, ferries [across]{para} in play.
Row, Ḍombī, row, Ḍombī, the road's come clear,
by the true [guru]{guru}'s feet I'll go back to the [Jina's town]{jinapura}.
Five [oars]{keruala} dipping at the prow, the rope tied behind,
bail with the [sky]{gagana}-scoop; the seams let no water inside.
Left and right, two ways; minding neither, row at will.
Takes no [cowrie]{kabadi}, takes no coin, ferries [across]{para} at will.
Who climbed a chariot can't row, sinks [shore]{kula-shore} after [shore]{kula-shore}.

couplets.kept: Rivers, boat and the plunging Mātaṅgī girl all stay; the inversion 'goes a boat' ends 1a on the image. 'Ferries across' returns word for word in 5a, as pāra karei does in the source. Gaṅgā, goes, girl alliterate.
couplets.letGo: 'There' (tahim̐) is cut; 'plunged in' carries it. The source does not rhyme here and neither does the English. The Tibetan's 'a river flows' is not sung: the boat follows the accurate English.

couplets.kept: The doubled call 'Row, Ḍombī, row, Ḍombī' opens on hard beats and stays identical each time. I sing the draft's chosen sense of uchārā, 'the way has cleared', as 'the road's come clear'; 'go again' becomes 'go back'.
couplets.letGo: The near rhyme uchārā/jiṇaurā: I found no honest English pair. 'City of the Jina' is sung 'the Jina's town' to shorten 2b, which still runs to about fourteen syllables.

couplets.kept: The full rhyme bāndhī/sāndhi becomes the slant rhyme 'behind'/'inside', with 'tied' chiming. Oars, prow, rope, sky-scoop, water and seams all stay, and the two participles 'dipping… tied' keep the list of boat gear.
couplets.letGo: 'At the stern' is sung 'behind' (piṭata, literally 'on the back'). 3b turns 'it does not get in at the seams' round to 'the seams let no water inside', so the seams become the subject.

couplets.kept: Halves built alike, as the source's are: 'Moon and sun, two wheels' / 'Left and right, two ways'. 'Creation and destruction' is sung 'making, unmaking'. Rebai is sung in its heeding sense, 'minding neither'. 'At will' recurs in 5a.
couplets.letGo: The near rhyme pulindā/chandā survives only as a faint echo, 'pulinda'/'will'. The articles before 'pulinda' and 'two ways' are cut, and 'as you please' becomes 'at will' to match 5a.

couplets.kept: 'Takes no cowrie, takes no coin' keeps the doubled refusal (… na lei … na lei). 'Ferries across' repeats 1b's phrase, and 'at will' echoes 4b, as succhaṛe echoes chandā. Chariot, rowing, sinking and the doubled 'shore after shore' stay.
couplets.letGo: No rhyme in source or English. 'She' is dropped, as the Bengali has no subject; 5b goes singular ('Who climbed… sinks'), as buṛai is, and drops 'at'. There is no self-naming to keep; see questions.

questions: Couplet 5 is marked as the bhaṇitā, but the Bengali as printed names no one. The Tibetan (Toh 2293) opens 5a with Dom+bi, perhaps reading ḍombī where Shastri prints boḍī, which would make this the poet's signature. If you adopt that, 5a would be sung 'Ḍombī takes no cowrie…' and lose 'coin'. I sang the Bengali as the accurate English stands.

Refrain 2b sings jinapura as 'the Jina's town' to keep the line near the length limit, but 'town' is the glossary's word for nagara (song 10). Keep it, or restore 'the Jina's city' at about fifteen syllables?

3b recasts 'it does not get in at the seams' as 'the seams let no water inside' to rhyme with 'behind'. If that turn is too free, the unrhymed fallback is 'bail with the sky-scoop; no water gets in at the seams.'

Refrain 2a follows the draft's reading of uchārā, 'the way has cleared'. If you adopt the draft's alternative ('it has grown late on the way'), the sung line would be 'Row, Ḍombī, row, Ḍombī, it's late on the road', and the cue stays the same.

4a sings srsti-samhara ('creation and destruction') as 'making, unmaking', and 5a/4b both sing 'at will' where the accurate English has 'of her own accord' and 'as you please'. Are these acceptable sung variants?
